ladder.analysis: The fight centers on whether Congress's power of the purse can be used to curb a war that began without a congressional vote. Because funding bills typically need 60 votes in the Senate, Democrats—soon to hold majorities in both chambers—currently have leverage to shape the Dec. 11 stopgap bill before they formally take control of Congress. That leverage is complicated by internal Democratic disagreement: some lawmakers, like Kaine and Van Hollen, want to use the deadline to force war-funding restrictions, while incoming committee chairs DeLauro and Meeks worry that triggering a shutdown would only disrupt unrelated government services without actually ending the conflict. Republicans, meanwhile, are split between seeking a bipartisan deal and turning to reconciliation—a process that would let them pass funding, including for military operations, without needing Democratic votes at all.

stories.headline: Russian missile hits Poland during Ukraine strikes as NATO scrambles jets
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on AP, AFP
body: Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region. Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow. Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border. The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact". The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents. Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz. He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday. A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine. "It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday. Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy". In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable". European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end. The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.

At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea. This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv. Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack. Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine. The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

stories.headline: Trump says Putin ready for diplomatic end to Ukraine war; US floats NATO membership for Kyiv
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on AP
body: President Donald Trump said Russian President Vladimir Putin 'clearly expressed' a desire to end the war in Ukraine by diplomatic means, following a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trump described the talks as 'very good' and said he believes 'there’s a real good chance' an end to the war can be reached. The summit, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, produced what Trump called a 'declaration of peace,' though European leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed skepticism about the prospects for a lasting settlement.

Speaking at a press conference after the Shenzhen talks, Putin said the Americans were 'insistently' asking Russia to allow European participation in peace negotiations. Putin claimed Russia was not opposed but wanted to clarify 'what Europe will bring to these talks,' and said Moscow had invited European leaders to come to Moscow to determine their positions. He also said he had discussed a 'possible ceasefire in a number of areas' but decided against it after a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge. Putin insisted Russia is 'interested' in ending the war and ready to make compromises, but accused Ukraine and Europe of not being willing.

U.S. envoy Jared Kushner, who attended the Berlin summit of Ukraine’s allies known as the Coalition of the Willing, told reporters that Trump wanted to make a deal with Moscow 'with Europe by his side.' Kushner said the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of U.S. envoys that the Europeans should be at the table, and that Moscow was now 'comfortable' with Ukraine having security guarantees based on NATO’s Article Five collective defense clause. Reports indicate U.S. negotiators have mulled giving Kyiv such guarantees without full NATO membership, if Ukraine agrees to territorial concessions.

European leaders meeting in Berlin expressed readiness for talks with Russia but struck a cautious tone. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Europe has 'a clear and consistent and united negotiating position,' while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's 'maximalist demands are not realistic.' Merz said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence were unacceptable, rejecting a 'Yalta format' for peace. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk took exception to Trump calling Putin a 'friend,' saying 'Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be.' French President Emmanuel Macron urged allies to do the 'maximum' to deliver air defense systems to Kyiv and to 'reopen the question' of Ukraine’s NATO membership.

Zelensky, speaking after the Berlin summit, said there is a 'huge chance' the war will end 'if the United States will really pressure Putin.' He called on global superpowers to 'stop trade with Russia,' pointing to China as Russia’s most vital economic partner and noting that the Trump administration has expanded business with Moscow despite sanctions. Zelensky said Ukraine faces 'a difficult winter' but hinted at possible changes in U.S. policy when Trump’s party loses its majority in Congress in January. He also said details of the next prisoner-of-war exchange between Kyiv and Moscow have not yet been finalized.

The trilateral summit in Shenzhen coincided with continued Russian attacks on Ukraine. As delegations met in China and Germany, several buildings in Kyiv’s historic center came under drone attack, killing one person and damaging the Dutch and Austrian embassies and Saint Volodymyr’s Cathedral. Russia continues to pound Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as winter sets in, and Kremlin officials have not budged from demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory. Putin’s aide Yury Ushakov said a 'great deal' would have to be done before the negotiating format could be expanded to include Europe, suggesting further rounds of discussions are needed.

stories.headline: ICJ rules Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya, orders reparations
body: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the country's Rohingya community, marking the first time the United Nations' top court has found a state responsible for genocide. In a 9-6 decision, the 15-judge panel determined that Myanmar's security forces killed at least 10,000 Rohingya people, perpetrated widespread sexual violence, committed acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing civilians during a brutal 2017 military crackdown that drove more than 730,000 Rohingya to neighbouring Bangladesh. The court ordered Myanmar to prevent a repeat of the crimes, undertake legal reforms to protect the Rohingya, and provide reparations and restitution, including facilitating the safe, voluntary and dignified return of those who fled, returning or replacing stolen property, and compensating victims where restitution is not possible.

The case was brought by The Gambia seven years ago, accusing Buddhist-majority Myanmar of a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya community in 2016 and 2017. Myanmar had argued its actions were legitimate counterinsurgency operations against the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA), an armed group that had attacked police and military posts. The ICJ flatly rejected this, with President Yuji Iwasawa stating that casualties and damage were "far in excess of what was justified by military necessity." The court said the "only reasonable inference" from evidence of widespread atrocities was that Myanmar's forces had the intent to destroy a "substantial part" of the Rohingya minority, and that Myanmar violated its obligation to prevent genocide by allowing armed civilians to participate in the military campaign.

Rohingya activists hailed the ruling as a historic validation of their decades-long persecution. Lucky Karim, who fled her village in 2017 at age 14 and heard the judgment in person at The Hague, called it "a very personal day." Wai Wai Nu, a former political prisoner and Rohingya activist, said the ruling "permanently shattered" the state-sponsored lie that the military's actions were merely clearance operations. Tun Khin, a Rohingya activist and plaintiff in a universal jurisdiction case against Myanmar in Argentina, described it as "a historic moment" and "a big day for the Rohingya." The Gambia called the ruling "a historic day for international justice" and urged Myanmar to comply fully and without delay. The Myanmar government did not respond to requests for comment, and the state-run New Light of Myanmar newspaper made no mention of the ruling online.

The judgment is the first finding of genocide against a state by the ICJ and only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court has ruled that the crime was committed. Michael Becker, an associate professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin, said the ruling was "monumental" not only for finding a state responsible for genocide but also for demonstrating that establishing genocidal intent is not impossible. The court took pains to show that The Gambia's case passed the "only reasonable inference" test for genocidal intent, and the ruling affirmed that forced transfer, targeting children and sexual violence could be relevant factors.

Attention quickly turned to the challenge of enforcing the court's remedies. Those behind the genocide, including former military chief and current president Min Aung Hlaing, have remained in power since toppling Myanmar's democratically elected government in 2021. Much of the country, including Rakhine State, is in the midst of a brutal civil war, and the Arakan Army, which controls most of Rakhine, is widely accused of persecuting the Rohingya as well. Enforcement ultimately falls to the UN Security Council, but China and Russia, which both back the Myanmar government, would "almost certainly" veto any proposed resolution to punish Myanmar, said Richard Horsey, senior Asia adviser at the International Crisis Group. The UK immediately expelled Myanmar's defence attache in London and called for an urgent UN Security Council session to discuss the judgment.

Rohingya activists acknowledged that real change will be long and difficult. "A judgment in The Hague will not on its own stop the bombs or feed starving families or stop the atrocities in Rakhine State," said Wai Wai Nu, urging the international community to take action to enforce the ruling. Lucky Karim said other countries should use the ICJ judgment "as a tool to open every possible door to help us and protect the people on the ground." The Gambia's lead counsel, Arsalan Suleman, said the genocide ruling could be used to hold perpetrators to account in other courts, including the International Criminal Court, which is weighing an arrest warrant request for Min Aung Hlaing for alleged crimes against humanity. Tun Khin said most Rohingya simply want to return home with full citizenship rights and legal protection, but acknowledged, "It will take time. This is just the beginning."

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin hold first trilateral summit at APEC, release peace declaration
body: The leaders of China, Russia and the United States held an unprecedented trilateral summit Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, and issued a joint peace declaration that made no mention of the ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran. Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin met for about one hour and 20 minutes. Trump told the two leaders, 'We are really making history,' while Xi described the talks as 'fruitful' and Putin called them 'open and candid.'

The declaration affirmed that 'a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought,' language previously used by the five permanent U.N. Security Council members, but stopped short of proposing a framework for denuclearization. Xi called for nuclear weapons to 'be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them].' The document also prioritized 'promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges,' increasing the production and supply of refined petroleum products, and protecting diplomatic immunity. It stated that 'the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction'—a clause benefiting Putin, who faces an ICC arrest warrant.

Analysts described the summit as largely symbolic. 'Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,' said Prof. William Hurst of the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back, saying, 'It is a serious collaborative work.' Hurst added, 'This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power.' Patricia Kim of the Brookings Institution said, 'The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation.'

European allies voiced indignation at the optics. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, 'Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be.' Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called it 'very incomprehensible' that Trump would meet Putin. Trump and Putin had held a separate bilateral meeting earlier, their first since August 2025, where Trump called Putin his 'friend.' Trump and Xi also held their third bilateral meeting of the year, during which Xi described U.S.-China relations as 'generally stable and positive' but cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the U.S. 'must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks.' Xi also called for enhanced communication on AI to 'ensure that AI remains under human control at all times.'

Separately, Trump faced accusations of falling asleep during Xi’s speech at the main APEC summit. Video showed Trump appearing to close his eyes and tilt his head downward for roughly 10 seconds. White House communications director Steven Cheung denied the claims, stating Trump was 'looking at papers in front of him' and accusing media of lying. Administration officials have previously attributed similar apparent drowsiness to blinking or listening intently, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio testifying he had 'never seen' Trump fall asleep.

stories.headline: Global tech sell-off deepens as Anthropic falls after IPO, Nvidia extends losses
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters, AP
body: A deepening sell-off in technology stocks accelerated Friday, dragging major indices lower and darkening the outlook for the remainder of 2026. The Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, particularly those tied to the artificial intelligence buildout, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory. The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%. On prediction market Kalshi, traders now place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026, down from 72% on Oct. 13.

The sell-off was fueled in part by the disappointing debut of Anthropic, the frontier AI laboratory that raised $81 billion in its blockbuster IPO by selling shares at $83 each, above the expected range. The stock is falling on Friday, taking the broader market with it. Nvidia, the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom, extended its losses after CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China. Nvidia's stock had already fallen 33% from its Oct. 6 peak through Thursday morning. The company named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.

The broader market is also absorbing a structural shift in corporate behavior. According to an analysis by Acadian Asset Management, U.S. corporations have switched from net repurchasers of shares to net issuers, adding supply to a market that had benefited from a shrinking share count. As of late last week, net new issuance equaled 3.1% of total market capitalization. Recent deals include Oracle's filing to sell $20 billion in stock, Meta's $25 billion common-stock offering, Alphabet's $84.8 billion equity raise, and SpaceX's $85.7 billion IPO. The trend has reversed a dynamic that helped boost prices, with increased supply now acting as a headwind on the bull market.

Nvidia's troubles have raised concerns about its role as the so-called 'central bank of AI,' given the hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments it has made to support the AI ecosystem. These include up to $36 billion in commitments to buy cloud services from smaller AI companies known as neoclouds, a $105 billion phased guarantee for a data center project in Ohio, and a promise to backstop up to $125 billion of a $500 billion credit program by Wall Street firms. Columbia Business School professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh estimates the total obligations at roughly $400 billion, a fraction of Nvidia's roughly $3.9 trillion market capitalization even after its decline. Analysts and former regulators, including former FDIC head Sheila Bair, say Nvidia is not 'too big to fail in a bank sense,' but caution that a serious disruption could still be a 'seismic event.'

The risks flowing from AI are drawing close scrutiny from financial officials. The IMF's Global Financial Stability report in October warned about growing leverage among AI firms and investors, noting that hyperscalers have grown from 1% to 10% of the $15 trillion investment-grade debt market in just two years. If the value of Nvidia's GPU chips fell, it could prompt questions about whether companies that borrowed to buy them could repay their debts, potentially creating reinforcing effects between the economy and financial markets. For now, most neoclouds' equity prices have recovered this week as Nvidia's share price has fallen, suggesting investors see Nvidia's problems as company-specific. The Stock Trader's Almanac, in a Thursday note, said 'the market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out,' though it left open the possibility of a 'Santa rally' later in December.

stories.headline: Fed officials signal rate hikes as inflation persists, AI boom adds pressure
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Federal Reserve officials have intensified public debate over the path of interest rates, with most agreeing that rates should be raised soon but disagreeing on the pace, as inflation remains above the central bank's 2% target and the artificial-intelligence boom adds economic heat. The increasingly vocal discussion comes as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has deliberately avoided signaling his own policy views, a stance that some analysts say is encouraging more, not less, commentary from other members of the Federal Open Market Committee.

According to a Bank of America analysis cited by CNBC, there has been more so-called Fedspeak in the past two weeks than in any similar period since the start of 2025. Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave said in a note Thursday that Warsh's refusal to guide markets 'might be encouraging the rest of the FOMC to speak more, not less,' adding that 'absent this leadership, both sides might feel incentivized to speak more often and more forcefully.' The minutes from the Fed's October meeting, at which the committee held rates steady, hinted at tension over Warsh's communication philosophy, with some officials who favored a hike saying they could have supported a hold 'provided that it was clearly understood by market participants that further tightening was likely.' Market veteran Ed Yardeni wrote Thursday that Warsh's approach 'may thus be limiting the Fed's flexibility precisely when it needs it most.'

Among the most hawkish voices is Governor Christopher Waller, who has raised the possibility of a half-percentage-point hike at the December meeting. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem has also entertained more aggressive hikes over a shorter period. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, who voted against the October pause in favor of a quarter-point increase, recently tried to thread a needle between transparency and forward guidance, saying her observations were 'not promises' and 'not forward guidance' but 'a conditional set of expectations.' Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee expressed sympathy with Warsh's view that the Fed should avoid being 'forward guidance-oriented' and making 'falsely precise' pronouncements, but stressed that each FOMC participant should explain how they see the world. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson defended the variety of voices, saying 'volume is not the same as clarity' and that the mixture 'guards against any single communication becoming the only one that matters.'

Financial markets have interpreted the cacophony as hawkish. Traders are pricing in a 100% probability of at least a quarter-point rate hike in December, with a small chance of a half-point move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch. Odds are high for a follow-up increase in January and possibly one more before the end of 2027. Current inflation indicators are running above 3%, but market measures of longer-term inflation have declined, with five-year forward expectations through the Treasury market at their lowest since April. Bhave warned that the 'back-and-forth is undue rates volatility in already turbulent times.'

Meanwhile, the AI boom is adding a new dimension to the Fed's calculus. At a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday, Warsh said the U.S. economy is 'at a hinge point' and publicly questioned whether AI could produce a 'China shock' for service workers, lowering prices but causing severe job losses. AI lab Anthropic is planning to price its IPO on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation, and vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to consider raising rates in December to slow price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy. Warsh has assembled a task force on AI, drawing expertise from outside the Fed, including venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, who said heavy regulation in healthcare and education means technology cannot rapidly displace jobs in those sectors. The task force is expected to produce a report for Warsh in the coming months, after which the Fed will debate whether the technology's potential to lower prices in services might eventually warrant lower interest rates over the long term.

stories.headline: President Trump Posthumously Pardons Pete Rose
body: President Donald Trump announced Thursday that he has granted a posthumous pardon to baseball legend Pete Rose, who died in September 2024 at age 83. In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote, "I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND." Trump also praised Rose's record of 4,256 career hits and 17 All-Star selections, though he incorrectly described the total as "4,256 Hits in a Season." Rose accumulated the hits over his 24-year MLB career; the single-season record is held by Ichiro Suzuki, who had 262 hits in 2004.

Rose was permanently banned from baseball in 1989 after an investigation found he bet on the Cincinnati Reds while playing for and managing them from 1985 to 1987. He admitted to betting on baseball in his 2004 autobiography. In 1990, Rose pleaded guilty to two counts of filing false tax returns, failing to report $354,968 over four years. He was sentenced to five months in prison, fined $50,000, and ordered to perform 1,000 hours of community service, which he carried out as a gym teacher's assistant with inner-city children in Cincinnati. He also repaid the Internal Revenue Service.

Rose's MLB reinstatement came posthumously in May 2025, when Commissioner Rob Manfred removed all deceased players from the league's permanently ineligible list. Manfred acknowledged that Trump partially played a role in that decision. The reinstatement makes Rose eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame; the earliest he could be inducted is 2028, under the "Classic Baseball" category for contributions before 1980. The next vote is scheduled for December 2027 at MLB's Winter Meetings.

A 17-time All-Star and three-time World Series champion, Rose spent 19 seasons with the Reds, winning World Series titles in 1975 and 1976, and added a third championship with the Philadelphia Phillies in 1980. He was National League Rookie of the Year in 1963, NL MVP in 1973, and World Series MVP in 1975. He won three NL batting titles and holds the record for most games played (3,562). As manager of the Reds from 1984 to 1989, he compiled a 412-373-1 record. The Cincinnati Reds inducted Rose into their own hall of fame in 2016 and retired his No. 14.

In his Truth Social post, Trump also criticized Rose's exclusion from the Hall of Fame, writing that Rose and former pitcher Roger Clemens were "treated terribly" and adding, "Politics, I guess!" The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital. Rose's absence from the Hall of Fame has long been debated; in what is believed to be his last interview before his death, Rose told KTLA, "I was absolutely 110% wrong for what I did … and that's bet on baseball games, and now you're punished for the rest of your life."

stories.headline: Colts release quarterback Daniel Jones after lackluster performance
body: The Indianapolis Colts released quarterback Daniel Jones on Friday, a day after a 26-3 loss to the Houston Texans on Thursday Night Football. Jones completed 12 of 27 passes for 144 yards with an interception in the defeat, which dropped the Colts to 3-8. Head coach Shane Steichen announced the move and declared that Anthony Richardson will be the starter moving forward.

Jones signed a two-year, $88 million contract extension with the Colts in March that included $50 million fully guaranteed at signing. For the 2026 season, he appeared in 11 games, completing 58.4 percent of his passes for 1,974 yards, seven touchdowns, and 13 interceptions. According to Over the Cap, Jones has now earned over $158 million in career salary between the Giants and the Colts. The release creates $49.49 million in dead money and a $30.31 million cap hit for Indianapolis, per OverTheCap.

Jones, 29, was selected by the New York Giants with the sixth overall pick in the 2019 NFL Draft out of Duke. He replaced Giants legend Eli Manning as the starter in Week 3 of his rookie season. After a tumultuous tenure marked by turnovers and injuries, the Giants rewarded him with a four-year, $160 million contract in spring 2023 following a playoff appearance. He was benched after a 2024 loss to the Carolina Panthers in Munich, requested his release, and landed with the Minnesota Vikings before signing with the Colts as a free agent in 2025.

Jones initially played well for the Colts, but his performance declined after a loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers and his 2025 season ended early with a torn Achilles. This season, he failed to throw for multiple touchdowns in any game and never finished a game with more touchdowns than interceptions. According to CBS Sports' Doug Clawson, among 678 quarterbacks who started each of their team's first 11 games over the last 45 years, Jones is the only one who never had a single game with more passing touchdowns than interceptions.

The Colts turned down trade interest from the Vikings and Ravens ahead of this year's deadline, according to Adam Schefter. Minnesota instead acquired Kirk Cousins, while Baltimore brought in Jacoby Brissett. Just 11 days before the release, Tom Pelissero reported that the Colts informed Jones he would not be traded. Jones will now be subject to the waiver wire; any team claiming him would take on his remaining $2 million salary for 2026 and $38 million in non-guaranteed money for 2027.

Richardson, the No. 4 overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft, entered Thursday's game with seven minutes left and did not complete either of his pass attempts. He will make his first start since the 2024 season when the Colts host the New York Giants on Nov. 29. Steichen had told reporters after Week 10 that Jones would remain the starter, and ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported earlier in the week that Steichen was "not motivated" to play Richardson unless absolutely necessary.

stories.headline: Measles outbreaks surge in U.S. as Georgia sees record spike
body: Georgia is experiencing a record spike in confirmed measles cases as the United States grapples with widespread outbreaks of the disease, which was officially declared endemic in the country this week after an international body determined the airborne virus has returned and spread uninterrupted for at least a year. In 2026, there have been more than 5,400 U.S. measles patients, at least 11 of whom have died, while others face devastating long-term outcomes. Only 18 of this year's total cases have been imported; the rest are domestic. The surge is a stark contrast to the 85 cases reported in 2000, the year measles was declared eliminated from the United States, and a dramatic increase from the 59 U.S. cases confirmed just three years ago, according to CDC data.

Public health officials are also investigating a community measles exposure at UnityPoint Health – Meriter Hospital Emergency Department in Madison, Wisconsin. The exposure came from a person who lives in another Wisconsin county, visited the hospital, and later tested positive for measles. The exposure occurred from 10:32 p.m. on Nov. 15 to 12:50 a.m. on Nov. 16. Public Health Madison and Dane County said they are reaching out to people who were exposed but do not have a full list of everyone. Officials noted that vaccinated individuals are extremely unlikely to get measles but still need to watch for symptoms; anyone who is not vaccinated and has been exposed must quarantine starting Nov. 22.

The resurgence of measles is being described by infectious disease experts as an early warning signal that vaccination, surveillance, and public trust have all eroded, and that other preventable diseases are likely to follow. Rochelle Walensky, MD, MPH, who directed the CDC from 2021 to 2023, called the return of endemic measles an "embarrassment," a "significant setback," and "tragic," adding that it demonstrates that "vaccination, surveillance, and public trust have all eroded and other preventable diseases are likely to follow." Tom Frieden, MD, MPH, who led the CDC from 2009 to 2017, agreed, noting that as the most contagious disease known to humans, measles is "like a canary in the coal mine" for other vaccine-preventable illnesses. "It's the first to come back. But it's not the only thing that's happening," Frieden told CIDRAP News.

Falling vaccination rates for the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine—which is 97% effective after two doses—have allowed imported cases brought through international travel to snowball into large outbreaks. Experts warn that rubella and mumps could return in the next several years, and that pertussis (whooping cough) is already seeing a resurgence as coverage of the diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis vaccine (DTaP) has also dropped. William Schaffner, MD, an infectious disease physician at Vanderbilt Medical Center, said he anticipates mumps will appear first, noting that earlier this year San Diego State University reported a mumps outbreak among members of its football team. He also expressed concern about chickenpox and noted that a case of polio was reported in 2022 involving a healthy but unvaccinated 20-year-old man in New York who suffered paralysis. "It's very distressing, because there is a strong element of turning back the clock, or the calendar, to the bad old days," Schaffner said.

Paul Offit, MD, director of the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia Vaccine Education Center, said that with the elimination of endemic measles, the country also eliminated its memory of the disease. "I think people don't remember how sick or dead that virus could make you," he said, "so now people don't fear the disease." The last major rubella epidemic in the United States, in 1964–1965, led to 11,000 miscarriages and stillbirths, while another 20,000 babies were born with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS); 2,100 newborns died. Peter J. Hotez, MD, PhD, dean of the National School of Tropical Medicine at Baylor College of Medicine, said he has cared for two or three babies with CRS in his lifetime and would hate to see that return. Whooping cough, meanwhile, can be so violent that children sometimes fracture a rib or experience seizures, and a provisional CDC report found that 10 babies died from the disease last year.

Many experts have pointed to messaging from Washington, D.C., and specifically to Robert F. Kennedy Jr., secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), as contributing to vaccine skepticism. Kennedy has pushed back, stating in a Nov. 17 social media post that he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles and that the department is working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. However, critics note that Kennedy dismissed the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, replaced some members with vaccine skeptics, attempted to scale back the childhood vaccine schedule, and directed the CDC to rewrite its Autism and Vaccine page to imply that the link between autism and vaccines remains an open question—despite a preponderance of scientific evidence showing no such link. Offit, one of many calling for Kennedy's removal, said, "It's this see-no-evil approach. RFK Jr. is a very successful anti-vaccine activist."

stories.headline: Taung Child study suggests multiple ancient human ancestors coexisted
body: A century after its discovery, the 3-million-year-old Taung Child fossil is challenging long-held assumptions about human evolution. An international study led by Professor Gabriele Macho of Vrije Universiteit Brussel, published in Nature, dates the fossil to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years ago and finds that the ancient hominin family tree in southern Africa was far more complex than previously thought.

The Taung Child, discovered in South Africa in 1924, is the original type specimen for the species Australopithecus africanus. However, scientists never established definitive criteria for assigning later fossils to that species, leaving the Taung Child as the only fossil that can be identified with certainty as A. africanus. By examining tooth structure and patterns of brain and dental development, researchers found that several adult fossils traditionally classified as A. africanus followed developmental patterns different from those of the Taung Child—suggesting they may represent multiple distinct hominin species that inhabited the Sterkfontein region, either concurrently or at different times.

The researchers attribute this diversity to dramatic climate shifts that repeatedly transformed southern Africa between wetter and drier conditions millions of years ago. As habitats expanded and contracted, hominin populations moved, became geographically isolated, evolved along separate paths, and sometimes came back into contact and interbred. Changing conditions also exposed populations to different predators and pathogens, adding further evolutionary pressure.

Evidence from fossilized pollen shows that the region where the Taung Child lived was considerably wetter and more heavily forested than today, with tree species now found hundreds of kilometers to the northeast. This suggests the landscape was dramatically different from modern South Africa.

"For over 100 years, we assumed the Taung Child was just one of many similar fossils from the era," said Professor Macho. "Our findings turn that on its head. The human family tree wasn't a neat, straight trunk—it was a chaotic, tangled bush driven by climate shifts." The study, published in npj Palaeoecosystems (DOI: 10.1038/s44513-026-00008-2), indicates that the emergence of the genus Homo was preceded by a far more diverse and interconnected network of ancient human relatives than previously recognized.

stories.headline: Anthropic mathematician claims to prove Riemann hypothesis; founders cash out $2B in IPO
body: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of the company’s Claude AI, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. The Riemann hypothesis, first proposed in 1859, concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved, and is one of seven Millennium Prize problems administered by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently; Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in his announcement.

In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday. Alpöge’s statement says Claude was integral to developing the proof: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions.” The solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”

Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.” In the quarter-century since the Millennium Prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: the Poincaré conjecture. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids. OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt; the result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. The achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing. Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude.

On Thursday, Anthropic became a public company in the largest IPO on record, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. Each of the founders sold about 3.4 million shares at the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, pocketing about $280 million each before underwriting fees and taxes. Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money, saying each has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy, though the company points out these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”

In addition to selling its Class A common stock, Anthropic also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry: Nvidia bought $10 billion, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest. At the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic, having converted a small percentage of promissory notes as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake; had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%. The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic. The company needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026, and $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030, with a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future.

stories.headline: Nvidia's Huang resigns amid affairs; California subpoenas firm over China ties
body: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese national whom U.S. officials believe is a spy. California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced Thursday that the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia, probing whether the company or Huang facilitated the transfer of advanced GPUs or confidential information to China and whether investors were misled. “The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement.

The California investigation centers on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based AI infrastructure firm Megaspeed. Megaspeed purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years and has been separately investigated by the U.S. and Singapore over suspected illegal chip transfers to China; the Justice Department has since taken over that federal probe. Nvidia’s board has hired an outside law firm and an independent slate of directors to assess the damage, while the U.S. Congress is preparing to subpoena Huang, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil inquiry into Nvidia’s disclosures.

Beyond the China-linked affair, the New York Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him. Reuters then reported a third affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The Times also detailed a long pattern of alleged abusive management: Huang reportedly told subordinates that because Nvidia’s wealth made monetary motivation impossible, humiliation was the only lever. He was said to have told one executive his mother should have aborted him and threatened to rip another employee’s arms off. A former HR chief, Michael Winston, threatened to sue in 2005, calling Huang’s conduct the most abusive he had seen; Nvidia paid him over $1 million. Huang’s spokesman called the allegations fabrications.

The board accepted Huang’s resignation on November 12, appointing CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. Chairman Harvey C. Jones said the company has no intention of reinstating Huang, despite a public petition from thousands of employees and public calls from Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey, and Y Combinator President Garry Tan for his return. In his first public statement since resigning, Huang said he had seen an “outpouring of calls” for his return and would be “honored” to come back if the board deemed it in the best interest of shareholders and the company. Separately, Bloomberg reported that Huang appeared “broken and shattered” when he surrendered his role, and the Wall Street Journal reported he had described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer.

Nvidia reported quarterly earnings on November 17 that beat expectations, with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year. Kress said the company is on track to exceed full-year guidance and that customers and partners remain “100% behind us.” However, Nvidia announced it will stop selling its H200 chips in China, ending participation in a controversial loophole in U.S. export bans. Meanwhile, Democratic lawmakers have opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s handling of Nvidia chip sales to China, noting that Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported spy last fall but then granted permission for H200 sales in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of export proceeds. Huang has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee before Thanksgiving; the closed-door briefing is expected to be recorded and transcribed.

stories.headline: Google DeepMind says AGI threshold near, calls for preparation
body: Google DeepMind has published a report arguing that artificial general intelligence (AGI)—machines that match humans across nearly all cognitive tasks—is coming within reach, and that the field must now seriously consider the subsequent development of artificial general superintelligence (ASI). The company warns that AI could continue to advance at its current pace or accelerate, with profound implications for science, the economy, and society at a scale much greater than AGI alone.

DeepMind defines ASI as a system that consistently outperforms large groups of human experts on tasks that could take them years, using fewer resources and less time—for example, making the scientific progress of an entire research field in a fraction of the time or achieving technological developments comparable to what large companies produce in a year. The report frames general intelligence as a continuum, with human-level AGI as one point and ASI further along, noting that the theoretical upper limits of intelligence are well understood but that the vast space between human-level AI and those limits is largely uncharted.

A key driver of progress, according to the report, is what DeepMind calls 'cognitive industrialization'—the commoditization of cognitive work driven by rapid improvements in hardware manufacturing, algorithmic efficiency, and compute hardware investment. Over the past decade, global effective compute stock has grown by at least tenfold per year, a factor of 10 billion over ten years. Meanwhile, the compute demand for running an AI workload has fallen by about fourfold per year; a task costing $1 billion today could cost just $1,000 in ten years. Extrapolating these trends, DeepMind estimates that the effective population of today’s AI agents could scale up more than a thousandfold by 2030 and more than a billionfold within a decade.

The report outlines four potential pathways from AGI to ASI: scaling models and data (though it notes bottlenecks such as data exhaustion and diminishing returns on model scale); technological paradigm shifts beyond today’s transformer-based architecture; improving coordination among multiple AGI instances to create 'group agents' or virtual economies; and recursive self-improvement, where AI systems automate improvements to future generations of AI. DeepMind emphasizes that simply scaling up today’s human-level AI in speed and number might itself bridge the gap to weak ASI, but that missing capabilities—such as the invention of genuinely new concepts—may require deeper breakthroughs.

DeepMind stresses that preparation for this potential shift requires mapping the possible roads from AGI to ASI and building rigorous, reliable ways to track progress. While the outcome is far from certain, the report argues that with AGI now within reach, the question of what comes after can no longer be postponed.

stories.headline: Google gives Gemini the ability to control your Mac
body: Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf by navigating native Mac apps and browsing websites in the background. The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac along with a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. Google did not say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

Computer use is a type of agentic offering that lets an AI agent take actions directly on the user’s computer. In Gemini’s case, the AI can complete multistep tasks that involve getting things done across local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they will see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things. As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen.

Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, such as filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.

stories.headline: Google to retire Google Assistant on smart speakers and shut down Nest app in 2027
body: Google has announced significant changes to its smart home software, including the retirement of Google Assistant on smart speakers and smart displays and the shutdown of the Nest app, with specific dates set in 2027. The Nest app will be shut down on January 25, 2027, and Google Assistant will be replaced by the Gemini for Home voice assistant on August 2, 2027.

The Nest app shutdown means users will have to manage their Nest products—including Nest thermostats, cameras, and Nest Protect alarms—via the Google Home app. Google says it will automatically transfer Nest devices, cameras, and video history to the Home app on January 25, and will also move Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to Google Home Premium. The company will begin deleting Nest account data on March 25, 2027.

For the Assistant transition, Google argues that Gemini for Home allows users to ask more complex questions and speak naturally rather than using dedicated commands or specific language. Gemini for Home was announced last year, and Google also killed Google Assistant on phones earlier this year, making the smart home move less surprising.
Google says it plans to share more updates about the changes ahead of the August 2027 transition.
These moves mark the end of an era for Google Assistant on smart home devices and consolidate Google's smart home ecosystem around the Google Home app and its new Gemini voice assistant.
